stories.headline: Lockheed Martin to add 1,250 jobs in Douglas and Jefferson counties over eight years
stories.summary:
Lockheed Martin announced Thursday that its space division will expand operations at facilities in Douglas and Jefferson counties, adding 1,250 jobs over the next eight years. The new positions will include cybersecurity engineers, software engineers, technicians and administrative services staff. The announcement was made at the Site Selector Conference feedback dinner in Lower Downtown Denver, hosted by the Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce and the Metro Denver Economic Development Corp.

The Douglas County facility will receive 450 new jobs and 190,000 additional square feet of space. Lockheed Martin currently employs approximately 12,000 people in Colorado out of a global workforce of 125,000. The company has maintained a presence in Jefferson County since 1955 and is that county's largest primary employer.

Gov. Jared Polis praised the expansion, saying 'Coloradans are building the future of aerospace, and this expansion strengthens our nation-leading aerospace industry and our economy.' Kate Watts, vice president of Lockheed Martin space strategy and business development, credited the state and local community partnerships for making the growth possible. The company designs and engineers spacecraft including the Orion capsule used in the Artemis II lunar mission earlier this year.

stories.headline: Weiser and Marx meet for first and likely only Colorado governor debate at Chamber of Commerce forum
stories.summary:
Republican Victor Marx and Democrat Phil Weiser appeared together Thursday for the first — and likely only — forum of the Colorado governor's race, hosted by the Colorado Chamber of Commerce at the National Western Center in Denver. The event focused on business and economic policy, with candidates receiving questions in advance. Marx appeared to read from prepared notes throughout the forum, while Weiser said he did not use notes.

On the question of new state revenue versus fiscal management, Weiser called the framing a 'classic false choice,' citing overspending on Medicaid transportation and chronic underfunding of education. Marx said he would target administrative growth, outside consultants and duplicative technology for cuts, adding: 'Before the government asks for any more of our money, it should prove that it can actually manage our money.'

Marx has declined most traditional moderated debates since winning the GOP nomination and did not speak to reporters after Thursday's event. Weiser, the state's two-term attorney general, said afterward that he welcomes unscripted appearances and does not need questions in advance. The race for governor is one of the most closely watched contests on Colorado's November 3 ballot.

stories.headline: Victor Marx campaign spending draws scrutiny over payments to obscure Las Vegas consulting firm
stories.summary:
A CPR News investigation has found that Republican gubernatorial candidate Victor Marx's campaign paid $20,000 to Varyation Consulting, a Las Vegas-based firm with no apparent security expertise, a minimal online presence and ties to a Tokyo-based real estate broker named Varya Shozen. The campaign initially described the payments as covering security assessments for events but provided no specific breakdown despite multiple requests. Attempts to contact Shozen were unsuccessful.

Campaign finance expert Mario Nicolais described the expense report as 'very unprofessional and sloppy,' saying it reflects the hazards of not hiring experienced professionals. The Marx campaign has already faced separate complaints over erroneously accepting over-limit donations and potentially using its merchandise store to circumvent contribution limits, with the campaign now facing one of the largest campaign finance penalties in state history.

The investigation notes that Marx's campaign spending broadly departs from established playbooks for statewide campaigns in Colorado. The campaign responded to questions only through written emails and did not grant interview requests. The governor's race is scheduled for a November 3 vote.

stories.headline: Advance Colorado backs six ballot measures in November election, targeting taxes, energy, immigration and redistricting
stories.summary:
Advance Colorado, the conservative advocacy group that has repeatedly succeeded at Colorado's ballot box despite the state's Democratic shift, is backing six measures on the November 3 ballot — four proposed constitutional amendments and two propositions. The measures address income tax caps, natural gas rights, ballot language readability, congressional redistricting, and immigration enforcement notifications. Constitutional amendments require 55% approval to pass; propositions need a simple majority.

Among the most significant is Proposition 136, which would cap the state income tax rate and was filed as a counterweight to Amendment 87, a Democratic-backed measure that would create a graduated income tax raising rates on the wealthiest Coloradans while cutting them for most others. Another Advance measure would require law enforcement to notify federal immigration officials when immigrants without legal status are charged with violent crimes or new offenses after prior felony convictions.

Advance Colorado has drawn criticism for condensing complex policy into ballot language that critics say obscures far-reaching consequences for voters. The group has the backing of major Republican figures and donors but operates with limited public transparency about its funding and internal structure. This fall's slate is the group's largest single-election effort in recent memory.

stories.headline: CU Denver to open first public U.S. university campus in India
stories.summary:
The University of Colorado Denver announced plans to open a campus in India, which would make it the first public American university to offer U.S. degrees on Indian soil. The initiative represents a significant international expansion for the Denver-based institution and is expected to give Colorado students and faculty new research and academic exchange opportunities.

Details on the campus location, timeline, degree programs and enrollment capacity were not immediately available from the brief announcement. The move comes as U.S. universities have increasingly looked to establish footholds in India's fast-growing higher education market, which has seen rising demand for American-accredited degrees.

CU Denver is part of the University of Colorado system, one of Colorado's largest employers and research enterprises. The expansion could have implications for the university's standing as a research institution and for Colorado's broader profile in international academic and business circles.

stories.headline: Update: Rockies finish fourth straight 100-loss season at 58-104; team raises ticket prices 12%, reaffirms Monfort ownership
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies closed their 2026 season at 58-104, a 15-win improvement over the prior year but still a fourth consecutive 100-loss campaign — making them the first franchise to accomplish that since the 1962-65 New York Mets. The team went 8-30 over their final 38 games after appearing on track to avoid the century mark in losses. Manager Warren Schaeffer received a vote of confidence from club leadership.

Club president Walker Monfort confirmed the team will raise ticket prices approximately 12% for next season, describing it as an effort to close the gap between Rockies pricing and the MLB average. 'Obviously, coming off of another 100-loss season, that's not easy to justify,' Monfort acknowledged, adding that all business decisions are aimed at improving on-field competitiveness.

Monfort also addressed ownership structure, saying a sale of a majority stake is not being considered. The Penner Sports Group — owners of the Denver Broncos — made a minority investment in the Rockies in April to help clear pandemic-era debt. President of baseball operations Paul DePodesta said underlying metrics showed meaningful progress in 2026 but acknowledged more improvement is needed. The Chicago White Sox, who similarly lost 100 or more games from 2023-25 before making the playoffs in 2026, were cited as a model for the turnaround the Rockies are pursuing.

stories.headline: State report recommends Colorado acquire 10,000 acres of disputed San Luis Valley ranch
stories.summary:
A report commissioned by Gov. Jared Polis and authored by former U.S. Sen. Ken Salazar and consultant Berrick Abramson recommends that Colorado acquire approximately 10,000 acres of the 83,000-acre Cielo Vista Ranch in the San Luis Valley. The recommendation comes after months of negotiations between ranch owner William Harrison, who purchased the property in 2017 for $105 million, and the heirs of a pre-statehood land grant who have long contested access rights to the land.

The dispute stems from the 1844 Sangre de Cristo Land Grant, established through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which granted settlers and their heirs the right to hunt, graze and gather timber on the land. Harrison declined a state offer to purchase the entire ranch outright, and his counter-proposal — offering land-grant heirs expanded access to 10,000 acres in exchange for surrendering rights to the remaining 70,000 — was 'rejected quickly and decisively' at community meetings.

The report's recommended acquisition would open the 10,000 acres to public recreation while preserving existing land-grant rights on those acres and beyond, with no rights surrendered. Harrison is described as open to improving the parcel by spreading grass seed and upgrading roads. The report calls for a 45-day period to explore terms of a state acquisition.

stories.headline: Colorado expands teen driver education requirements starting January 2027
stories.summary:
Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Colorado will require all teens ages 15 through 17 to complete a 30-hour driver education course before obtaining an instruction permit, under a 2024 law taking effect next year. Those ages 18 through 20 must complete either the 30-hour course or a four-hour prequalification driver awareness program. Anyone under 21 seeking a motorcycle permit or endorsement must first complete a Colorado State Patrol-approved motorcycle safety training program.

The changes address a troubling trend: while Colorado's graduated licensing system contributed to a long-term 35% drop in total teen fatalities between 2002 and 2025, fatalities among 15-to-20-year-olds have risen 91% over the past decade, climbing from 45 deaths in 2015 to 86 in 2025. The new rules also require fingerprint-based background checks for driving instructors.

CDOT Executive Director Shoshana Lew said the expanded requirements are aimed at producing safer drivers and reducing crashes. Previously, teens who obtained permits at 16 or older were not required to take any educational course before the written permit exam. Families with teens approaching driving age should confirm enrollment in approved programs before the January deadline.

stories.headline: Denver Pioneers open college hockey season ranked No. 1 after sweeping Alaska Anchorage
stories.summary:
The University of Denver men's hockey team opened the 2026-27 college hockey season ranked No. 1 in the country after sweeping the University of Alaska Anchorage in their opening series. The Pioneers enter the season as the preseason favorite following a strong finish to the prior campaign.

DU hockey has been a consistent national contender in recent years, regularly competing in the NCAA tournament and drawing significant fan interest at Magness Arena. The No. 1 ranking out of the gate signals high expectations for the program heading into conference play.

The Pioneers will face increasingly competitive NCHC opponents as the season progresses. Denver's strong start will be tested against conference rivals in the weeks ahead.

stories.headline: Little Blue Pigeon Bookstore to host first Blue Book Festival on Larimer Square this Saturday
stories.summary:
Little Blue Pigeon Bookstore, which opened on Larimer Square on April 1, will host its inaugural Blue Book Festival on Saturday, Oct. 10, from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. along Larimer Street between 14th and 15th streets in downtown Denver. The free event will feature 30 Colorado authors, ticketed appearances by two New York Times-bestselling headliners, and free activities along the street. Several additional Denver-area independent bookstores will also participate.

Owner Paige Dungan, a former book publicist, said the event is intended to showcase Denver's broader literary community rather than promote a single shop. Little Blue Pigeon is notable for being Larimer Square's first dedicated bookstore in decades — possibly since the 1970s. The festival reflects a national trend: the American Booksellers Association reported 3,281 member locations in 2025, up from 2,844 in 2024.

The Colorado-based Mountains & Plains Independent Booksellers Association has seen membership increase significantly in recent years, with 18 new member bookstores opening in 2025. Dungan said she regularly directs customers to other local shops when she doesn't carry a title they seek, and views in-person author events as essential to sustaining readership.

stories.headline: Colorado seasonal mountain road closures begin; key passes and expected timelines
stories.summary:
Rocky Mountain National Park closed Old Fall River Road to vehicles for the season on October 6, marking the start of Colorado's annual high-elevation road closure season. Several other major mountain passes are expected to follow in the coming weeks, with closures driven by snowfall, avalanche risk and road conditions rather than fixed calendar dates.

Independence Pass, which connects Twin Lakes and Aspen, typically closes between late October and early November — it closed October 31 in 2024 and November 17 in 2025. Cottonwood Pass near Buena Vista usually closes in late October or early November, though a stretch near the Mount Yale trailhead often remains accessible. Guanella Pass, known for access to Mount Bierstadt, typically closes around Thanksgiving, while Kebler Pass is expected to close in late November to early December.

Mount Blue Sky Scenic Highway closed October 5 and typically reopens around Memorial Day. Routes including Berthoud Pass, Loveland Pass and Hoosier Pass generally remain open through winter except during extreme weather. Drivers planning mountain travel are advised to check current road conditions before departing, particularly as the region could receive early-season snowfall in the coming weeks.

stories.headline: 'Dancing with the Stars' live tour to stop at Ball Arena in March 2027
stories.summary:
The 'Dancing with the Stars' live tour will make a Denver stop at Ball Arena on Friday, March 19, 2027, as part of a 60-city North American run. The tour kicks off January 21, 2027, in New Hampshire and will for the first time include a full 'Dancing with the Stars' troupe alongside featured dancers.

Tickets for the Denver performance are available through Ticketmaster, with a presale option for fans who register in advance. The Ball Arena booking follows a series of major entertainment announcements for the venue in the 2026-27 season.

'Dancing with the Stars' has maintained a strong following in the Denver market. The live tour format gives fans an opportunity to see the television competition's professional dancers perform in person.

topStory.headline: Christa Pike Walking, Eating After Surviving Botched Tennessee Execution, Attorneys Say
topStory.summary:
Christa Pike, the Tennessee death row inmate who survived two doses of lethal injection on Sept. 30, is walking with assistance, regaining some movement in her arms and has begun eating again, her attorneys reported Thursday. The updates mark a significant turnaround from days earlier, when her legal team had described her as effectively brain dead following the failed execution at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.

Pike's attorneys described her recovery as "remarkable" and "profound," crediting the medical team caring for her. However, they cautioned that significant questions remain about long-term effects from the two doses of pentobarbital administered during the execution attempt, and that her arms remain severely swollen and of limited function. Her lawyers also noted she is experiencing cognitive difficulties including problems with concentration and memory, and that physicians say it could take months to determine whether those impairments are permanent.

Pike's legal team said she is grappling with the psychological aftermath of the failed execution, describing her as traumatized by "the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die." Despite that, her attorneys said she has expressed concern for the family of her victim, Colleen Slemmer, whose mother, May Martinez, witnessed the botched execution after waiting more than 30 years for Pike's death. Martinez has said Pike never apologized for the killing and that Pike's execution would have delivered justice for her daughter.

Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Slemmer, which she carried out alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp. Shipp, who was 17 at the time, was spared the death penalty on account of his age and remains in prison. Pike was 18 when the crime was committed. A court has ordered state officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution, which could form the basis of a future lawsuit against Tennessee.

Pike's attorneys have repeatedly called on Gov. Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison, arguing she has "endured more than enough" and should not face a second execution attempt. Lee has not responded to those calls. Speaking to reporters Oct. 1, Lee called the botched execution a "tragedy" but reaffirmed his commitment to carrying out death sentences handed down by Tennessee juries, leaving open the possibility that Pike could face a second execution. Legal experts have described Pike's situation as unprecedented, as she is believed to be the only person to have survived a lethal injection execution attempt.
